paragraphs.text:
[?]TATIONEM [?]

1. "Among those born of women none is greater than John," the Saviour's word declared. How, then, shall I offer a crown of words to one who received so great a crown from the Lord? How shall I praise him who learned the hidden mystery before he was born? For before his birth Christ [?] showed him the prelude of grace and entrusted [?] to him; to him he committed the treasures of grace. And the things the angels dancing in heaven did not know, John, as you have just heard, spoke through his mother while he was still being carried in the womb. This escaped the Thrones, yet God did not pass over the child in the womb; he hid it from the Dominions, yet revealed the mystery of the dispensation to the one in the belly. And the good news the archangel had come to bring, the unborn child proclaimed from within by leaping. For when the Redeemer of our race came to dwell among us, as you have just heard, he came to his friend who was being carried in the womb, while he himself had just been conceived.

2. One could see the Fashioner greeting the clay, the King lodging in the soldier's tent, the Master arriving at the servant's chamber. John, seeing him from one womb in another, saw ahead and, leaping, tried to overstep the bounds of nature, saying: "I do not know the bounds of nature, for I see the Lord who set the bounds of nature. I do not wait for the time of gestation in the womb. The nine months are not necessary for me, for the Eternal One is with me." What mother, then, persuaded God the Word to come and dwell visibly among us? Who acted as ambassador and roused from the Father's bosom the

And who is this Virgin, who appeared to God more honourable than all the po-

[Notes:] [?] Barb. reads "of Christ"; [the translator] seems to have read "God." [?] seems to have read "mystery." Cod. Barb. reads "they undertook."

-wers? Who is she that holds the Uncontainable in her womb? Who is she that carries the Unapproachable in her belly? Who is she that made it possible for the grass of humanity to bear the fire of the Godhead? Who will announce to the wife of our forefather Adam the mystery now being accomplished? Who will tell her that the condemned woman has come carrying the Judge within her? That the woman who heard "In sorrows you shall bring forth children" has come carrying the one who brings us release from sorrow? [?] Oh, the honour! Oh, the inexpressible change! God separated the first-formed man from paradise, and was himself contained within that man's descendant. He who sewed garments of skin in paradise is covered within a womb. He came to dwell in compassion in the very place where, in anger, he had cast out our forefather. He trod with his divine foot the earth he had cursed, annulling the sentence and crushing the thorn of sin with his spotless footsteps.

These are John's leapings, or rather his words, for the leapings of the child not yet born were words. Who among the wise of the Greeks, grey with age, has ever taught such things as the Forerunner proclaimed before he was in swaddling clothes? Such are the mysteries of the present festival. As I try to proclaim them, I shall find myself diving into a depth of wonders and walking on air as I tell of heavenly things. Therefore I beg you, Baptist: hold out to me the anchor of your prayer, and since you are a voice, keep my organs of speech from stumbling. For I have come believing, not doubting, to offer you the incense of words. Trusting in this, I shall recount your contests, and if I am defeated I shall rejoice, for it is victory for me to be overcome by the wonders of my patron.

4. "It came to pass," it says, "in the days of Herod the king." Let no one be robbed of the right interpretation because of the name in the Gospels. One Herod is the one who killed the Forerunner; another is this Herod who mowed down the green shoots of the infants while searching for the ear of piety. "In his days there was a certain priest named Zechariah, and his wife Elizabeth, and they were both righteous." For the woman shared a common life with her husband in good order,

so at once he held out to him a gentle voice, like a right hand, crying: "Do not be afraid, Zechariah." He first drove out his fear and only then announced the good news, so that Zechariah might receive the message with an untroubled soul. "Do not be afraid, Zechariah," he said, and then the good news his heart longed for: "Your prayer has been heard; your wife will bear a son, and you shall call him John. For I have come to you from heaven bringing not only a child but also the name of the one to be born; I have come having learned his name from the book on high. God has enrolled as a citizen one whom no womb has yet brought forth. 'Many will rejoice at his birth.' The child is yours, the shoot is yours, but the fruit belongs to all. You are the father, but the one to be born is a lamp for all."

7. When Zechariah heard this, he became at once overjoyed and curious. Receiving Gabriel's message with curious reasoning, he answered without faith: "How shall I know this?" Gabriel would not tolerate Zechariah's question. He scorned the priest who offered incense but had no faith, and, showing his indignation in his face, he said: "Are you demanding that I account for what I have said, Zechariah? Are you calling God's minister to account? Do you demand pledges from someone who brings good news? You receive the divine gifts not with thanksgiving but by putting them to the test, and you say, 'How shall I know this?' I am Gabriel. Take my name as a pledge of what has been spoken, and if that seems small to you, learn my rank: I am the one who stands before the Lord. And if you suspect me of lying, where will your accusation lead? I am the one who stands before the Lord, and you say, 'How shall I know this?' How will you know? 'For I,' you say, 'am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.' Priest, is time more sovereign in your eyes than the Creator of time? Will you not stop distrusting God and giving way to time, instead of saying, 'How shall I know this?' How did you learn that Isaac was born to Abraham? Because he believed, he overruled time. Was it not because he believed that old age obeyed? But if the barren woman's case seems impossible to you, how shall I entrust to you the mystery of the Virgin? If you have many examples and still demand pledges, how shall I recount to you the childbirth beyond words, of which Isaiah prophesied many generations before, saying: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son'?

He believed and proclaimed the greater thing; but you, disbelieving the lesser, demand an account from me, who was sent from heaven to you for your sake. But since you desire to receive a sign (for you asked for one, as you ought not to have done), receive speechlessness as the pledge of the childbearing: you shall be silent until the events confirm the words. Let the bonds of barrenness pass from the organs of generation to the organs of speech. Fettered in your voice, be pregnant for me with the Voice [?]. For to him alone will I grant pardon for his father's fault. He is the Master's friend; whatever he wishes, he asks as a friend."

8. While these things were being done and said within, the delay [?] filled the multitude with wonder, and their suspicions, divided in many directions, suggested to each whatever seemed likely, until Zechariah appeared and taught them by his silence what had happened to him. When he had completed the days of his service, he went home holding the good news in his inmost parts and a bridle in his mouth. This, one might say, was the beginning of the Forerunner's conception. Wishing to proclaim his birth, I must of necessity [touch on?] the neighbouring feast [?]

9. For in the sixth month of the conception Gabriel came to Nazareth, bringing the Father's good news to the Virgin. Seeing her at home, he greeted her first: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." "Hail," he said, "you who are the first and only one to bear a babe free from the curse. Hail, you who bring forth for the world the source of life. Hail, you who are [?], yet not childless. Hail, you who are unwed, yet not without offspring. Hail, you who are unsown, yet not without fruit. Hail, you who await pains [?] yet will have no birth-pangs. Hail, you who carry a protector for your forefather Adam. Hail, you who without toil carry the foundation of creation. Hail, you who without pain mediate for mortal nature. Hail, you who bear God not bare, and man not mere. Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you."

[Isa. 7:14 (?)] [Luke 1:28] [ibid. [?]]

[Jo]seph [?]. "I am not led astray by a voice; for it was to the first-formed woman alone, they say, that the author of evil spoke." And the angel said to her: "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace," the grace the first-formed woman lost. She alone received the deceit; you alone have brought the undoing of the deceit. "You will bear a son, and you shall call him Jesus." When she heard of a birth and a son, she said: "How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?" She was not contradicting him but seeking to learn by asking: "How will this be for me? Am I alone to make nature new? Will the ordinary means of childbearing be set aside in me? Tell me the manner, stranger, for your good news is strange."

11. "The Holy Spirit," said Gabriel, "will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." "Receive, Virgin," he says, "what has been said, and do not pry into what has been kept silent. I bear witness to the birth; the manner I leave aside. I have come to you as a messenger, not as a teacher of the dispensation; I was sent as herald of the Master's coming, not as its interpreter. How will this be? The 'how' is known to him who is present. That he is present I know, for the evidence within you leaps forward; but the manner I cannot tell. That I am no liar, Elizabeth will testify for me, who in barrenness and old age is carrying the Forerunner of the one within you. And if I have said that she is with child in barrenness and old age, that is no small pledge. For between an aged barren woman and a virgin there is no difference as regards giving birth."

12. When the Virgin heard this, she went to Zechariah's house, and finding Elizabeth with child, she greeted her. Mary greeted Elizabeth, and the babe answered from within; for the mother's hearing became the hearing of the unborn child. And since John, confined by the bounds of nature, could not speak, he spoke to his own mother by leaping, uttering his words through his leapings, and answered the Saviour's mother through his mother's tongue. Elizabeth, unable to contain the leapings of her child, was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out, saying to the Virgin: "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. You,

she says, are blessed, who carry the undoing of the curse. You are blessed, who bring the gift of wisdom. You are blessed, who are carrying the one who walked in paradise. You are blessed, whose womb has become a holy temple. Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb, by eating of which Adam will conquer the enemy. Blessed is the fruit that has become food and clothing for the world. 'And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?' These things, Virgin, the unborn child has taught me from within, leaping beyond nature at your greeting." Such were the God-inspired [words] of Elizabeth.

13. Zechariah, meanwhile, as I said, remained at home wearing the bridle of unbelief. He had received speechlessness for the same length of time as the pregnancy, and accepted the birth of the child as the limit of his sentence. When the citizen of the desert came forth from the desert womb, the father asked for a tablet and wrote with good sense what he had heard without faith; and when he had given the child his name, he received back his voice. Such, Forerunner and Baptist, are your mysteries before birth; such is the dignity God granted you before your conception. For Gabriel announced both the Master's birth and your conception; in the temple, as in a bridal chamber, he proclaimed your conceiving. The archangel brought your birth to the temple at a festival as a gift pleasing to God. You became a bearer of the Spirit, receiving the gift of prophecy in the womb, and by leaping you spoke within the belly what God revealed to Moses in his old age. Therefore the Bridegroom of the Church called you greater than the prophets. For which of the prophets proclaimed a mystery from the womb? Which of the righteous, on being born, offered his father a voice as a guest-gift? But you at one stroke freed your father from speechlessness and made him worthy of prophecy. For he who a little before had been speechless was filled with the Holy Spirit and proclaimed to us a song, which I shall strike up in a form suited to the occasion, altering it slightly. He says: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel"; but I say: "Blessed be the God of the Christians." To him be glory to the ages of ages.

[...] concerning the Forerunner; but now the Forerunner leads us to the one he proclaimed. If the birth of the Forerunner gladdened us, let the birth of our common Saviour gladden us still more. For the one only ran ahead to proclaim; but this one has come to save. John exists because of Christ, but Christ exists not because of John but because of the Father.

2. Let us come, then, to the exposition of the words of the Gospel. For the same archangel ministers both at John's birth and at the Saviour's conception. There the husband of the barren woman receives the good news; here a Virgin is taught. The archangel is sent no longer into a temple, as in John's case, but to the living temple, the Virgin.

[?] There Zechariah the priest went in to offer incense and heard the fragrant words of the archangel; here there is no longer a temple, but the Virgin is the temple. The angel does not come to the high priest; he comes to her who bears the heavenly High Priest. There the archangel came at the time of the liturgy; here not at the time of the liturgy, for the one to be born was going to put an end to bodily worship. There the archangel comes to the father; here he does not come to Joseph, who did not become a father, but to the Virgin, who became a mother without a father. There were Elizabeth and Zechariah; here Mary alone. For Joseph was her husband as one betrothed; he kept the virgin a virgin. So the archangel does not come to him, but to the

3. And what does he say to her? "Hail, full of grace," because God had said to Eve, "In sorrows you shall bear children." "Hail, full of grace," for Eve's sorrow is undone. Eve bore children in sorrows; this joy, then, undoes that sorrow. That is why he said: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." For he who a little later came forth from her was with her.

4. "But she was greatly troubled at the saying." For it was not a woman greeting a woman; a citizen of heaven was addressing a woman on earth. "She was troubled at the saying." Perhaps also because it was a man's voice, for the holy woman was unaccustomed to the greetings of men. So she stood still, startled at the voice, "and considered within herself what sort of
[...] let us celebrate. [...] is contained in a womb and is formed [?]; the [?] and saving [...] that leads all mortals back up to the things above. Let us faithfully celebrate the conception.

1779 ANTIPATER OF BOSTRA

[...] greeting this was" [?], "what this might be."

5. And the angel said to her: "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God; and behold, you will conceive in your womb." "You have found grace" was common, for others before her had found grace. But to say "you will conceive" was no longer common; it belonged to this promise alone: "and behold, you will conceive in your womb" — a virgin! A strange thing! "You have found grace with God": the one to be born had of necessity to come from a virgin, and you have been preferred above the other virgins.

6. "For you have found grace with God, and you will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus." When the virgin received the angel's greeting, she was in anguish and kept pondering; but when she hears the word of good news, she is no longer anxious about the word but perplexed about the promise. And she says to the angel: "How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?" She does not disbelieve the word; she asks about the manner. Zechariah disbelieved; but the virgin does not disbelieve. He said, "How shall I know this?", for he was seeking a sign in order to believe. But the virgin said: "How will this be? The word is trustworthy, but the manner is beyond me; nature does not know what you are speaking of. For 'behold, you will conceive' pointed to the present; it was not waiting for a husband. How will this be? Eve did not conceive before Adam came together with her. This is the order of nature, this the course of childbearing, this the law of succession. How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?"

7. Since she asked rightly, the angel said to her: "You are pardoned for your perplexity." He did not pardon Zechariah but silenced him for wrongly disbelieving; but he pardons the Virgin, for there was no precedent for a Virgin. "You are pardoned for your perplexity, since this has never happened before; with you it begins, and with you it will end. And I will tell you the manner too: do not expect a husband; do not wait for union with a man. The flesh will come without flesh, the child without union. In what manner? The Holy Spirit will come upon you." Hear spiritually what is said about the Spirit. It is without seed, by the descent of the Spirit; for what comes to be is constituted by the will of God.

8. "The Holy Spirit will come upon you." How will he come upon you? You will not [see?] him coming; he will act without appearing. "The Holy Spirit will come upon you." Why does the Holy Spirit come? Since holy indeed

…you are [a virgin], but you must become holier. For when a carpenter takes wood, or a smith iron, he still cleans it and works it to make it better suited to his craft. So you too were a virgin, but you must become holier, so that you may conceive the Holy One. 9. “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” He names two: the Holy Spirit and power. What is the power? Christ, the power of God. So the two come: the Holy Spirit and Christ, the only-begotten of God. “Since what is born of you will be called holy.” See, I pray, how she heard the whole: Holy Spirit and power [?]. The angel left nothing out; he passed over nothing in silence. “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and [?] the power of the Most High will overshadow you”: it will surround you and clothe you, it will be all around you and fence you in, and it will be a shelter for you. 10. Holy Spirit, Power, Most High: count up these things for me, and you will find everything precisely stated. For what are they? A human being on earth; an angel in heaven; the Holy Spirit, and the Son, and the Father. Once you have gone up to the source, you can go no higher, for he is the Most High, above whom nothing appears. So in the account of the Son's birth he joined everything together; everything had a share in it and came together into unity. For only these exist: angel, human being, Holy Spirit, Son and Father, and besides these there is nothing else. Leave aside, I pray, the irrational animals, which exist for the sake of man. They have no share in reason; they do not sin, are not judged, do no right, are not praised, and have no eternal life; they come into being here and perish here. But man is a rational living being, the most kingly of living beings, a citizen of the world, lord of the things made for his sake. Since, then, only these exist (man, angel, Holy Spirit, Son and Father), see how these things are joined together. The human being is the Virgin, a virgin setting right the fault of a virgin: you have the Virgin as the human being. The angel is Gabriel. The Holy Spirit is the one who comes upon her. The power of the Most High is the power that overshadows. See how, in the account of the Lord's birth, all that exists came together. The angel came down to the Virgin; the Holy Spirit comes upon her; the power of the Most High overshadows her; the Most High himself begot the Only-begotten and arranged for him to be born also of a Virgin, so that the one who fell in the beginning through Eve might himself be saved through the conception of the

11. “And the angel answered and said to her: And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son.” He gives the Virgin a sign: the conception of the barren woman. “And this is the sixth month for her, for with God no word will be impossible.” It is God who is at work; do not doubt. “And Mary said: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” I am the handmaid of the Lord, a tablet being written on: let the writer write what he wishes. The material is ready; let the craftsman do what he wills. “And the angel departed from her”: he received the words of faith and departed. “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” The Virgin did not say, “Away with you! What you say is absurd. I am a virgin; I do not know a man; what you say makes no sense.” But since the angel had said, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” she, being spiritual, heard spiritually; being holy, she believed the holy words in a holy way. She remained, keeping her faith and awaiting the promise. So the angel departed from her. 12. “And Mary arose in those days and went with haste into the hill country” to her kinswoman. Mary came to Elizabeth just as Christ came to human beings. Elizabeth ought to have come to Mary; that would have been the more fitting order of things, for the mother of the Forerunner to come to the mother of the Master. Yet Mary arises and goes to Elizabeth: she who was bearing the Lord goes to the mother of the servant. 13. “And she entered the house of Zechariah.” Since the angel had said to her, “Behold, your kinswoman has conceived,” she went in to rejoice with her, because she had conceived against all expectation. “And she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And it came to pass, when Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting…” She passed it through her ears to her mind, and her mind passed it to the Forerunner. The Forerunner heard before he had ears; he heard not by the workings of the mind but by the working of the Spirit. And the Forerunner leaps to show his joy and to signal prophecy: “and the babe leaped in Elizabeth's womb.” And Elizabeth understood the matter. She did not understand it by human reasoning; she grasped it by the Holy Spirit, the

14. “And she cried out with a loud voice and said: Blessed are you among women.” Why do you greet me? Why are you the first to address me? Am I the one bearing the Saviour? I ought to have come to you.

Another has conceived before you, and [another] will conceive after you [?]; [you are] a virgin among women [?]. But in the whole race of women [?] you alone are blessed in this way. “And blessed is the fruit of your womb”: not the fruit [?] of a husband, for what is born comes not from [a man?] [?] but from your womb. 15. See what the mother of John utters, filled with the Holy Spirit. “And [?] why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” [?] She sees a virgin and calls her mother, anticipating prophetically [?] by the word [?] and [?] being called mother [?]. Although she herself had conceived long before, she calls mother the one who is still a virgin. And she became [?] the forerunner of the Virgin [?], as John was of the Saviour. And Mary received good news from every side: from an angel

[?] of the Spirit, through the words of her kinswoman. She too is struck in her mind and moved like her by the same Spirit, so that the angel too [?] … as the word passed swiftly into deed [?], the Spirit having begun to come upon Mary. 17. When at one moment, in the same place, it was seen at work in two women, a barren woman and a virgin, the barren woman took the lead, since she had conceived earlier, and called the Mother of God blessed, while the virgin followed, since the one

[?] being proclaimed, she was conceiving. And one craftsman, the Holy Spirit, set two lyres sounding, [?] two souls of holy women: for Elizabeth was pronouncing her blessed, [?] and Mary [?]: “My soul magnifies the
18. First she shows that she believes the things spoken to her, because of the words, “Blessed is she who believed that” [?] my soul

“there will be a fulfilment of the things spoken to her by the Lord,” as she says: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Next, she does not return the blessing, so that things that differ so greatly may not be made equal. For what comparison is there between a slave and his master, or between a soldier's rank and a king's dignity? So she is called blessed, but she sends the praise up to the Lord, saying, “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Being a virgin, she was conceiving in her womb bodily, contrary to common nature: bodily, as in a body, but spiritually, since it was without intercourse. Yet since what was so wondrously arranged took place in a body, she says, “My soul magnifies the Lord.” “For even if God, as he promised, works wonders in my body,” she says, “still my soul is not fruitless toward the Lord. My body will bring forth a very great fruit, Elizabeth, as you said; for you said to me, ‘Blessed is the fruit of your womb.’ But this fruit is not the achievement of my own choice. It is the achievement of God, who works in me things beyond nature. I must also offer the fruit of my choice, so that not only my body may bear fruit, but my soul too may bring the fruit of its free choice to God, who works wonders in me.” And she says: “My soul magnifies the Lord”: not only my body, but my soul as well. “For the greater the wonder and achievement I serve, the more I am bound to be the first to glorify the one who works marvels in me.” 19. “And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour”: for God is my Saviour. “My spirit”: she names her own soul in two ways. “My spirit has rejoiced,” she says, “since I am counted worthy of such things.” “In God my Saviour”: that is, God, who graciously gives the world a Saviour from me. “For he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid.” “For who am I, for so great a work? He looked upon me; I did not expect it. I was lowly and cast aside, expecting nothing but the coming of a husband. Instead of a husband the Holy Spirit comes; I pass from earth to heaven and am drawn into an ineffable dispensation. That is why ‘he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid.’”

20. “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.” She calls herself blessed too, not speaking from her own tongue but showing the taste of the Holy Spirit who had come upon her, and prophesying she says: “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed”: not you alone. For what generation

from that time on does not call Mary blessed, she who knew nothing of marriage with a man but bore God by the Spirit? The word of prophecy came first, and the outcome proved true to the word. 21. “For the Mighty One has done great things for me.” How could they not be great things? “Being a virgin, I conceive; by God's will I have passed beyond nature, and without a man I am counted worthy not simply to be a mother, but to be the mother of the only Saviour.” She says “the Mighty One” because someone might disbelieve the working of the conception. “For if a virgin conceives,” she says, “it is because the Mighty One has done great things for me.” With the name “Mighty One” she drives out disbelief about what is contrary to nature, so that people may ascribe the achievement to the power of the one at work, and so that no one, by examining what does not follow nature, may fall away from true assent to what has truly taken place. And she adds: “And holy is his name.” “For his Only-begotten is not defiled because he comes into a woman. His name is holy, since I too am a holy Virgin. Nor is the Saviour conceived in me, the virgin, stained in any way as he forms his own body. For the Holy One bears his own handiwork in holiness. That is why the Holy Spirit also comes upon me: so that the conception, being made holy, may make the birth holy as well. Holy, then, is his name.” 22. “And his mercy is from generation to generation.” “I conceive, and he bears a body; he comes into the world, lives among human beings, conducts his life here below, and arranges all things, so that the unworthy may receive mercy, those who are unworthy because of the [?] of their sins.” “To those who fear him,” however. Those who are utterly unworthy do not receive mercy, but those who through repentance are turned to fear. 23. “He has shown strength with his arm”: the hand is his, and the work is not man's. “He has scattered the proud.” Whoever behaves arrogantly and thinks he needs no repentance is scattered. She is hinting at the people of the Jews, who would be scattered because of their pride against the Saviour. “He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.”

For each person scatters himself by the very things he imagines, becoming unworthy of the call of Jesus. 24. “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly.” The Pharisees and scribes thought highly of themselves and sought the chief seats, and they were brought down from them because they opposed Jesus. “And exalted the lowly”: those who had been scattered abroad, since they believed in the one who came from heaven and from on high. “He has filled the hungry with good things.” For the human race was starving, except for the Jews. “And the rich he has sent away empty”: that is, the Jews, who had grown rich through the giving of the Law and the teaching of the holy prophets. They fought for their pride and were greatly puffed up by their privilege, [refusing?] [?] to approach humbly the one who became man. So they were sent away empty, carrying nothing away: neither faith, nor knowledge, nor hope of good things. They have lost both the earthly Jerusalem and the life to come. 25. “He has helped his servant Israel.” She does not name [?] it; she means the true Israel: not those who pride themselves on the name, but those who have kept the faith that the name implies. “In remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to Isaac and to Jacob, and to his seed for ever.” She brings the prophecy to fulfilment, not only her own but also that of the prophets, according to God's promise that the common Saviour, Jesus Christ, would be born of her. So Mary prophesies nothing inferior, since she serves the most perfect dispensation, and her spirit rejoices in the Lord. Let the Church also rejoice in her Bridegroom and Saviour. For if Mary rejoiced even before the work came to pass, how much more ought the Church rejoice, now that she is betrothed and has already received the seeds of the holy Bridegroom through the teaching of the angelic words? She ought to rejoice still more, exult without ceasing, give thanks beyond measure, and win approval by works of virtue pleasing to Christ the Saviour who has come. To him be the glory and the power to the ages of ages. Amen. OF ANTIPATER [?], bishop of Bostra: from the Refutation of the Apology for Origen by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, first discourse, which begins: “For my part I thought I had written enough, and had done sufficiently what your holiness had enjoined [?]” [Manuscript note: the codex reads ὧν. The codex reads μὴ δέν.]

“…most God-beloved and most holy father John, in all things.” And a little later: Since the man was very learned, having searched out and tracked down all the books and writings of the ancients, having set out the opinions of almost everyone, and having left the world a great many writings, some of which deserve every acceptance, they rely on this reputation of his and try to carry some people away. “Eusebius,” they say, “would not have chosen to take this view unless he knew for certain that all the opinions of the ancients intended it.” I for my part agree and acknowledge that the man was very learned and that none of the older writings escaped his knowledge. With imperial assistance he could easily gather to himself what was to be found anywhere. But I do not say that the man attained precision in doctrine. So we must grant him wide learning, but not knowledge of doctrine; indeed, we know that he fell far short of such precision. And shortly after: So, lest we seem to be attacking the man over matters we do not intend to discuss at present, [we propose] to examine with precision the apology he made and to show that both are heretics: the apologist himself and the man for whom he composed the apology. And after other things: Show us one of the illustrious teachers of the Church who clearly and unambiguously laid it down as doctrine that human souls pre-exist, and do not try to offer sophistries as proof. As for your eagerness to show that some have spoken as he did of the Son's subordination to the Father, in the first place we are not surprised, for this is the opinion of you and your circle. So we will not discuss it at present, since it was long ago submitted to an ecumenical inquiry and condemned. [We are] not to be persuaded in this [editor's suggestion: nor ought one to be persuaded by this], nor to examine the people on whose account we have taken this up. But as for finding fault with the mere expression “On First Principles”, you have never yet heard that from anyone, you clever advocate of Origen's absurdities. BY THE SAME. From the discourse on the woman with the flow of blood, which begins: “That the first calling was of the Jews, Scripture has taught.” And after other things: The woman with the flow of blood said these things as she took hold of the saving fringe, laying hold of the Lord as king of nature and telling of the tyranny of her affliction. And when she had obtained the gift, she raised a statue to Christ: she had spent her wealth on physicians, and she offered what was left of her wealth to Christ. BY THE SAME. From the work against Origen. For the devil, though he had the same immortal glory as the angels, did not keep his own dignity

and rank. He was cast out of his own place and fell from the glory of God, yet he remained what he was by nature, immortal, and likewise in power, no less than what he had received in his nature from God at the beginning. But he is now prevented by God from using this force and from carrying out against us the wrath against our race that he acquired out of envy, since God provides for us and guards us from his wickedness as long as we are worthy of God's care. But if through negligence we are found unworthy of his help, then the devil displays his wickedness and power against us, whenever we have become entirely bare of good works and made ourselves strangers to God's providence. As long as we are worthy to be joined to the help that comes from God, he is in no way permitted to advance against us. The swine at Gadara bear witness that the demons had no scope for doing harm even against them until it was permitted. That permission they received at that time for many and various purposes of God's dispensation, which there is no time to list at present. [?] of Origen's treatise, chapter [?]. BY THE SAME. From the discourse on the cross. The request to be spared death belonged to the human will of our nature in Christ, about which he says, “Not my will be done, but yours.” For as God he indicated beforehand that the cup would pass from him. He rose on the third day, having made the flesh immortal and shattered the [?] of death

BY THE SAME. From the discourse against Apollinarius. He who suffered for us not only committed no sin, but tore up the very roots of sin from their foundations. So it is not as one opposed to God that he says, “Not my will be done”; rather, he is giving us patterns for how to pray to God in times of temptation. Apollinarius, because of the words “Not my will be done,” does away with the intellectual part of Christ's soul, and in his mindlessness proclaims an incarnation without soul or mind. But if the will to live is an insult to Christ, it is far more insulting to say that Christ became a curse and sin, was tempted by Satan for forty days, fled from Herod into Egypt, was subject to Joseph the carpenter, and was strengthened by an angel as though he feared death.

[?] Dalmatius [?] of the holy [?] at Cyzicus [?]. Of Dalmatius, archbishop of the holy and catholic Church at Cyzicus [?]. A letter sent to the holy synod in the city of Ephesus by Dalmatius, the most holy archimandrite. I received the letter sent to me by the holy synod, and when I learned what it contained, I was first of all deeply grieved at the hardships and afflictions that have come upon you. For it was written in the letter that some of the holy fathers staying there have died because of the harsh conditions. For the rest, know that I am ready to carry out your every command. In nothing have I overlooked or do I disregard anything, nor have I neglected anything, especially since the matter concerns the orthodox faith and is pleasing to God. For no one can depart from the living God and make other plans. Those who rightly handle the word of God's truth have life both in this age and in the age to come; but those who depart from the grace of God are accursed, cast into the [?]
